pr_title: kernel: Prevent deadlock on rare k_thread_abort() / k_thread_suspend() corner case
pr_body:
When k_thread_abort() or k_thread_suspend() is issued at ISR level, and the target thread is active on another CPU, then the caller must spin while it waits for the target thread to be halted. This works as long as at least one of the CPUs was operating at thread level.
    
However, when _all CPUs involved_ are operating at ISR level, and trying to abort (or suspend) active threads on other CPUs, a deadlock scenario can occur because they are ultimately waiting for another CPU to perform a context switch--a context switch that will not be performed until an ISR exits.
    
If such a scenario is detected, we work around it by skipping the call to z_sched_switch_spin() and thereby breaking the deadlock.

Fixes #64646
pr_comments:
@andyross - I finally got around to digging further into the volatile issue. I built and for the following SMP boards: qemu_x86_64, qemu_cortex_a53_smp and qemu_riscv32_smp. Reading through the disassembled output for each of them, I have observed in each of them the problematic code (pre-fix).

qemu_x86_64:
```
  104e87:       83 e0 60                and    $0x60,%eax
  104e8a:       84 c0                   test   %al,%al
  104e8c:       75 fc                   jne    104e8a <z_thread_halt+0x12c>
```

qemu_cortex_a53_smp:
```
    40007804:   121b0400        and     w0, w0, #0x60
    40007808:   35000000        cbnz    w0, 40007808 <z_thread_halt+0x18c>
```


qemu_riscv32_smp:
```
8000449a:       0607f793                andi    a5,a5,96
8000449e:       e381                    bnez    a5,8000449e <z_thread_halt+0x15e>
```

The key takeaway from each of the above code snippets is that if the compiler is caching the thread state in a register and spinning on a value that will not change. If the current proposed fix is still flawed, I can make this into its own PR.

Key updates:

1. Introduce a sequence ID for SMP threads. This can be used to help determine with high confidence whether a pointer to thread is still the same thread or a re-used thread.
2. The deadlock detection used in z_thread_halt() now distinguishes between threads that are a part of the deadlock and those that are affected by it.  In the following link pattern, T is affected by the deadlock, but A and B are a part of the deadlock : T -> A -> B -> A).
3. When the ISR must spin waiting for a thread to halt, we do not spin on the thread data as it is possible for that to be stale/invalid data (as the thread may abort and get re-used).

Just getting back to this:

> Introduce a sequence ID for SMP threads. This can be used to help determine with high confidence whether a pointer to thread is still the same thread or a re-used thread.

But... now this isn't an actual solution.  The code we have **already** works almost always, except that sometimes it fails; and this has the same property.   That's not to say that one can't have that kind of code, but solutions like that[1] need to come with an analysis showing that the failure is "effectively" impossible for some set of practical assumptions.

Really: we just can't be inspecting the thread struct after we know it's on its abort path.  The shared data to detect the abort needs to live elsewhere, like on a atomic counter in the kernel struct or whatnot.  I have a vague sense I might see how this would work.  If I can find time this week I might try to throw something together myself.

[1] e.g. UUIDs: they don't technically guarantee uniqueness, but you can prove that the expected collision rate is e.g. longer than the expected lifespan of the sun.
(Oh, and I just realized that there's a corrolary requirement: a thread can't legally touch **its own** thread struct after releasing the lock on its way back out of the abort code.)

Or to put another way ... there is a basic problem is z_sched_switch_spin() being called from within the ISR that I was not addressing. After the target thread has aborted and a new thread has been scheduled on the other CPU, the current CPU can not assume that the memory pointed to by the target thread is _still_ a thread while spinning in z_sched_switch_spin().

> After the target thread has aborted and a new thread has been scheduled on the other CPU, the current CPU can not assume that the memory pointed to by the target thread is still a thread while spinning

Almost, you can't assume a general thread is still a thread, like e.g. the pointers you find in the spinning-on list.  You **can** make assumptions about the target thread being halted, because that's a pointer held up-stack by our caller.  Nothing in the system will be re-using the thread memory until we return, because that would be an application bug (i.e. calling k_thread_create() before k_thread_abort() had returned).

Hmmm ... with the _keep_spinning_,  I am beginning to think that we don't even need the z_sched_switch_spin() in this case at all and that it might resolve the deadlock on its own. Double checking as the scenarios can get tricky to properly parse.

Think I got it.  See #70455 

Basically no need for being fancy, just invert the loop and test for our _current being asynchronously halted every iteration.  Now all aborts get handled in finite time and no need for things like deadlock detection or mucking with threads with indeterminate lifetimes.

We don't need to detect deadlock to know that we don't need to call z_sched_switch_spin() in the ISR case. I don't think that we need to do it period with this proposal. This should also eliminate previously discussed issues about accessing the thread structure post-deletion.

Does it work more simply than the inverted loop?  I'm all for dueling and picking a winner.

Though we absolutely do need the switch_spin call before returning.  If we don't do that, then there's a race where the caller gets e.g. a return from k_thread_abort() and then re-spawns a new thread, whose switch handle then gets clobbered by the outgoing context switch on the other CPU, which appears to resume from the dead.  Yes, this was a real bug and it was outrageously difficult to figure out.  The dance with the switch handle and the semi-complicated docs around it in arch-interface.h are the result.

z_sched_switch_spin(), if in the execution path for both CPUs is going to cause a problem for the ISR deadlock scenario as each will be waiting for the other to finish. However knowing that it was introduced to solve the race you described is also valuable. We are both getting closer to putting the final nail in the proverbial coffin of this problem.

Slept on it last night, and I am thinking that z_sched_switch_spin() is insufficient.  We need the more in how we sync.  I am thinking that we really need the ability to sync CPUs during scheduling (z_sched_switch_spin syncs threads). I have some more thinking/modelling to do, but the core of what I am exploring is a multi-stage action.

1. Add a field to _struct_ __cpu_ whose bits indicate the CPUs upon which it must wait to save their outgoing thread.
2. Update arch_switch() to clear the bit in the other CPUs when it is done saving its own outgoing thread, and then have it spin until it is no longer waiting on any other CPUs before loading the new thread.

I am not yet convinced that the above is _the_ way to go. It is a starting point. I still have to work through suspend/resume because some work would need to be done there--especially to cover cases where at ISR level the same thread is both suspended and resumed. This also suggests that a thread returning from an ISR--even if there is no rescheduling--may have to perform that CPU spin described above.

Think I hit on the same basic idea.  The core roadblock is that we need to wait (in switch_spin) for the other side to write to the thread struct before returning from k_thread_abort (but not suspend, actually -- only abort leaves the thread in freed-memory state).  But (1) the write that it's going to do is actually constrained to happen at ISR exit time at a spot we have some control over, (2) the suspend case doesn't actually have that race and we can return before the context switch (since the thread is still live and active) and (3) in the case of abort, **we don't actually need to write to that thread struct** since the thread is dead anyway.  We just have to fool the arch layer into writing into a dummy thread, which is something we do at startup anyway; the trick is known to work.

Don't have time this afternoon, but might try tonight unless you beat me to it.

Had another epiphany here: this isn't really best understood as a deadlock bug at all.  Consider the case where an SMP/arch_switch[1] architecture does a k_thread_abort() of _current in an ISR, then a k_thread_create() on the same thread handle.  Totally legal, right?  The new thread struct has the switch handle for its initial context filled in[2] and is ready to go.  But then you return from the ISR... and the context switch then clobbers that field with the saved one from the dead thread that got interrupted!

The deadlock is just the result of a naive attempt to avoid one variant of this problem, but the core issue is fundamental and still present.

The solution shouldn't be hard: change the API to require that the arch layer re-read the _current pointer on exit and save to that instead of the original (most arch's cache _current in a register across the ISR).  Then provide (as mentioned above) a dummy thread in the CPU struct somewhere to store the switch handle of the dead thread.

Will see if I can get something up this week.  I'm actually on vacation so time is a little limited.

[1] Actually older architectures might well have the same issue, but with switch it's easy to detect portably because of the switch handle field.

[2] Or it might even start running somewhere else.
FWIW, we do not allow the creation of a thread from within an ISR--we have an explicit __ASSERT() for that.

>  FWIW, we do not allow the creation of a thread from within an ISR--we have an explicit __ASSERT() for that.

Ah, right (though IIRC there's no good reason for that beyond legacy API limitations).  Doesn't matter though, another CPU might do it: abort the thread and free the memory it was allocated from (or put it back in the queue, or whatever: anything to signal the rest of the system the memory is available).  Then another CPU happens to pick it up before the ISR exits and clobbers it.   The free memory condition is actually fundamental: k_thread_abort() promises the thread is available, and it's not until the ISR exits.

Have this mocked up now and it's a tiny patch.  The gotcha is that a bunch of the architectures are caching _current in a register across the ISR and don't re-read it from the CPU struct, so aren't sensitive to the thread change and write into the free memory anyway.   Can probably do all that myself, it's just boilerplate.  Though getting all the arch folks on board will extend review.
Dropping this PR as a potential solution in favor of https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/71185

issue_context.title: k_thread_abort() can deadlock on SMP systems
issue_context.body:
**Describe the bug**

There is a corner case in SMP where a deadlock can occur when terminating threads via k_thread_abort() from an ISR. 

**To Reproduce**

This was found through code inspection (not from a failing test case)

It requires two cores both simultaneously executing at ISR level and attempting to terminate the other core's interrupted thread. Below is the sequence of events. (This sequence will need to be updated slightly after PR #59400 is merged, but it would still result in a deadlock).

1. CPU0 executing thread0, CPU1 executing thread1
2. CPU0 enters ISR, CPU1 executing thread1
3. CPU0 ISR doing stuff, CPU1 enters ISR
4. CPU0 ISR issues k_thread_abort(thread1), CPU1 ISR issues k_thread_abort(thread0)
5. (Each CPU is now trying to abort the other's interrupted thread)
6. CPU0 ISR gets sched_lock, CPU1 ISR spins on sched_lock
7. CPU0 ISR determines thread1 is not aborting, CPU1 still spinning on sched_lock
8. CPU0 ISR sets thread1's _THREAD_ABORTING, CPU1 still spinning on sched_lock
9. CPU0 ISR determines that thread1 is aborting and it's not _current, CPU1 still spinning on sched_lock
10. CPU0 ISR determines it is in ISR, CPU1 still spinning on sched_lock
11. CPU0 ISR unlocks sched_lock, CPU1 gets sched_lock
12. CPU0 ISR spins while thread1's _THREAD_ABORTING is set, CPU1 ISR determines thread0 is not aborting
13. CPU0 ISR continues to spin, CPU1 ISR sets thread0's _THREAD_ABORTING
14. CPU0 ISR continues to spin, CPU1 ISR determines that thread0 is aborting and it's not _current
15. CPU0 ISR continues to spin, CPU1 ISR determines that it is in ISR
16. CPU0 ISR continues to spin, CPU1 ISR unlocks sched_lock
17. CPU0 ISR continues to spin, CPU1 ISR spins on thread0's _THREAD_ABORTING

Both CPU0 ISR and CPU1 ISR are deadlocked waiting for threads to abort

**Expected behavior**

Deadlock should not occur.

One possible solution to this would be to add some code to detect the deadlock and then act accordingly. This could be modifying the k_thread_abort() API to return -EDEADLOCK and let the caller handle it. Or it could be offloading the k_thread_abort() from ISR level to a high priority/metaIRQ thread that terminates it.

There may be yet another alternate solution.

**Impact**

Although this could hang the system, the likelihood is very low as it requires very specific circumstances (SMP + two or more cores in an ISR + each of those ISRs trying to terminate the other core's interrupted current thread)

It does not affect uniprocessor systems.
comments:
Cool, thanks.  Just commenting to register my opinion that this isn't actually possible given that the aborting flag is only set/checked from within the scheduler lock, which serializes access to the various k_thread_abort() invocations.   But who knows, this stuff is hard.

FWIW it wouldn't be too terribly difficult to write a stress test as a reproducer: two threads sit in a loop spawning/joining one other "victim" thread each.  The victims then (1) do a irq_offload() call (or some other trap, but this is easiest) to an ISR handler that is responsible for aborting the other victim thread then (2) exit.

Run this for a few hours overnight across a bunch of instances (half as many as you have host CPU cores -- it does need to be reliably getting two CPUs for SMP).  If there's a deadlock, it should show up.  And if not we can probably write it off as "so rare it's below the noise level of other failures", which is something at least.

Attaching a test case to replicate the issue. This test spawns two threads (one for each core). Each thread enters an ISR via irq_offload(). The two ISRs sync and then issue a call to k_thread_abort() to abort the other core's interrupted thread.

[Debug.zip](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/files/13220182/Debug.zip)

Once the project has been unzipped ...

```
$ cd <project>
$ west build -p -b qemu_x86_64 ./ -t run
```

Observed output ...

```
*** Booting Zephyr OS build zephyr-v3.5.0-728-g9fd0185c3b40 ***
isr_var1: 0x11e26d 0x10a000 0x11e26c
Spawned thread 0x10a360 is waiting
IRQ is syncing 0x11e26d
IRQ is waiting on 0x11e26c
isr_var2: 0x11e26c 0x10a360 0x11e26d
Spawned thread 0x10a000 is waiting
IRQ is syncing 0x11e26c
IRQ is waiting on 0x11e26d
IRQ is killing 0x10a360
IRQ is killing 0x10a000

```

Additional output is not observed. In a success case, we are expecting to see additional output that is something like ...

```
IRQ is done with 0x10a360
IRQ is done with 0x10a000
Final message!

```

If additional printk() statements are added into sched.c, we can see that we deadlock in z_thread_abort() -- soon to be z_thread_halt().

review_comments: This looks wrong to me: if you're grabbing the scheduler lock here, then that means it was released somewhere above, after the entry to the function (which starts locked).  If that happened, then the CPU running the target thread **may not be `cpu` anymore**, right?  All use of that returned variable needs to happen before the lock is ever released.

Good catch. In this version, I have restricted to the creation of the _spinning on_ linked list to CPUs that are in an ISR. Also, if the other CPU is no longer executing `thread`, then it should mean that the target thread has been both halted and swapped out, which should address the issue you raised.

Hm... this looks cleaner as it's not relying on a CPU pointer of a thread that might have migrated.

I'm still thinking I see a race though: once that lock is released, the other thread is free to abort or whatever, at which point it returns out to whatever context called k_thread_abort().  Now consider that context then **re-uses the thread struct** by (to be pathological) scribbling a halted value over the state bits.  Now this while loop can never return.

If we detect a deadlock like this, the various deadlocked spin loops need to be able to exit synchronously, with no intermediate states where one can be observed to happen first.

If I am following you correctly, we are no worse off on _that_ race than we were before. For it to occur, this ISR would have to be interrupted by something of even higher priority **and** take long enough for it to occur that the other CPU could context switch in a new thread **and** have some thread re-use the aborted thread's resources. Unlikely, but possible.

I _think_ I see a way to avoid spinning on the `is_halting(thread)`. There may be a simpler method available, but what I have in mind is a k_thread field that contains a bitmap whose set bits indicate which CPUs are spinning in an ISR waiting for the thread to halt and a _cpu field indicating that the target thread is entering a halted (suspended or dead) state. Instead of spinning on is_halting(), the ISR can spin on the new _cpu field until the halting thread indicates it can stop spinning.
